claims.text: The material family is multiphase Ni-based superalloys containing high concentrations of refractory elements such as Re and Ru.
These alloys will exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during aging at 600–800°C.
The non-monotonic ductility transition is caused by chemical ordering in the γ' phase followed by dissolution or coarsening.
The brittle condition coincides with peak chemical ordering of the γ' precipitates.
The initial solution-treated and water-quenched alloy contains a γ matrix and γ' precipitates.
The initial alloy has a high concentration or volume fraction of Re, Ru, and W.
The intervention is isothermal aging at 750°C for 10–1000 hours.
Mechanical testing is to be performed at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 after aging in vacuum or inert gas.
Chemical order and lattice-mismatch strain fields in γ' evolve from a disordered state to a highly ordered DO3 or L12 state and then to a coarsened or disordered state.
The alloy is initially ductile because the γ' precipitates are disordered.
Increasing chemical order creates strong anti-phase boundaries that impede dislocation motion and cause embrittlement.
Long-time precipitate coarsening reduces anti-phase-boundary number density and relaxes lattice-mismatch strain, thereby restoring ductility.
Elongation versus aging time will form a U-shaped curve with a distinct minimum.
The elongation minimum will occur at the aging time having the maximum γ' chemical-order parameter.
The transition requires sufficient refractory content to stabilize complex ordered phases such as DO3.
The transition requires an aging regime in which ordering kinetics are faster than coarsening kinetics, proposed as T < 0.8 Tm.
The temperature window of the brittle peak may shift with refractory-element composition.
Initial chemical ordering or TCP-phase formation may mask the proposed ductility transition.
The hypothesis is falsified by monotonic ductility or by failure of the ductility minimum to coincide with the peak γ' order parameter.
